html:
Headnote

Every Heading 1 becomes a section and a link in the side menu. Ingredients, Method, and Notes get their colors automatically.

A five-minute grain and a ten-minute pilaf. Onion and ginger do most of the work.1

a Side note in the margin. Make one: click at the end of the paragraph or step, press Enter, press Tab, type /callout. Side notes get letters a, b, c for you.

Ingredients

Heading 1 named exactly Ingredients, then bullets. Start each with an amount and a unit (cup, tbsp, tsp, g, oz, can, clove, small, pinch). The Serves buttons (from the Serves property) multiply the amounts. A line with no amount is left as is.

Serves
  • ½ cup fonio
  • 1 tbsp oil, for coating the fonio
  • 1 cup water
  • ½ tsp salt
  • 1 small onion, diced
  • Herbs and a lime, to finish

Method

Heading 1 named exactly Method, then a numbered list. Start each step with bold words.

  1. Cook the fonio. Coat the fonio with the oil, add the water and salt, cover, and cook on low about 5 minutes.1
  2. Build the base. Sauté the onion in a large pan for 3 to 5 minutes.
  3. Fold. Fold in the fonio and turn off the heat.

b Soggy? Cook off the remaining liquid. Dry? Add a spoonful of water.

To serve

Finish with herbs and a squeeze of lime.

Notes

Heading 1 named exactly Notes, then bullets.

  • Fonio is forgiving, so small changes in water are fine.
  • Make it a bowl with roasted vegetables.

Sources

  1. 1
    Yolélé Fonio, product packaging ↗ Brand
    Cooking time and yield, as printed on the bag.

title: Visual Research: Regenerative Agriculture Branding
dek: How a regenerative agriculture brand found its colors: two moodboards, 126,600 pixels, and almost no blue.
html:
The brief

Collecting materials for a client branding project focused on regenerative agriculture. The goal was a visual system combining earthy tones with living greens.

The clientA regenerative agriculture brand
The askLook like soil and growth, not like a wellness label
The guardrailVisuals can't promise more than the farming does. The Regenerative Organic Certified standard, set up in 2017, rests on soil health, animal welfare, and social fairness3.

Mood board & color study

Moodboards feel like instinct. I wanted to know what they actually said, so I measured them.

1

Collect. Two boards: one for color, one for texture and objects. Paper, seed packets, linen, soil, dried leaves, old maps, hand-drawn type. Anything that felt like it came out of the ground or out of someone's hands.

2

Measure. Every pixel on both boards got sorted by hue, in narrow bands around the color wheel1. The result looks like this:

What the boards said

Mostly neutral
about 48 percent of every pixel was paper, linen, bone, or shadow1.
Warm and narrow
92 percent of the remaining color sat between red-orange and olive, 10 to 70 degrees1.
One loud band
40 to 50 degrees, ochre and mustard, held 19 percent of all pixels on its own1.
No blue
the whole blue range came in under 1 percent1.
3

Extract. Next, the boards got reduced to their most common colors1. The bright white board background is left out.

Extracted palette
Paper#ece7da · 14.9% of pixels1
Wheat#c2b89b · 13.6% of pixels1
Soil#6f5e49 · 13.1% of pixels1
Loam#392315 · 12.3% of pixels1
Linen#d7d5c7 · 10.9% of pixels1
Dry sage#9b967b · 10.4% of pixels1
4

Correct. The measurement showed a gap. The boards had soil and paper, but no living green. So the working palette adds it on purpose, and every swatch gets tested next to the others, never alone. The same color reads differently depending on what surrounds it2.

Bark#8b7355
Canopy#2a5934
Clay#d4a574
Stone#c9b8a8
Sage#5d7d63
Linen#f5f0e8

Typography & texture studies

Exploring serif and sans combinations and texture layers that evoke soil, growing systems, and regeneration.

Regenerative Futures

Building Systems That Heal

RoleChoiceWhy
DisplaySerif, set large in SageFeels rooted and a little old, like an almanac
LabelsSmall caps sans, tracked wideBorrowed from seed packets and field tags
BodyPlain sansStays readable on packaging and small screens

Image references

Visual language: agricultural landscapes, soil close-ups, hands in earth, growth stages, water systems, community work.

Photo direction: real people, real dirt, natural light. No staged farmers in clean overalls.

Further reading

2017 · Regenerative Organic Alliance
Regenerative Organic Certified ↗
The standard behind the claims: soil health, animal welfare, and social fairness.
Sept 2026 · The Operating System

The research side: mapping where food grows, moves, and fails to arrive.

title: Fonio: A Small Grain With a Long Memory
dek: A tiny West African grain that cooks in five minutes, forgives your mistakes, and carries thousands of years of farming with it.
html:
The relic

Fonio is easy to overlook. Each grain is tiny, and a bag of it looks more like sand than supper. But it has been prized across West Africa for more than 5,000 years1, and in Mali it is known as the seed of the universe, the grain at the root of all existence1.

This piece keeps it the way a reliquary keeps a relic: described, traced to where it comes from, and handled with care.

Catalog entry
ObjectFonio, a small grain
Also known asThe seed of the universe, in Mali
RegionWest Africa
Kept forMore than 5,000 years
Cooks inAbout five minutes
Yield1 cup dry makes about 4 cups cooked

Description

Fonio is an ancient grain1. Cooked, it turns light and fluffy, with a gentle nuttiness1. It is also gluten free2.

Provenance

Brands like Yolélé, co-founded by Senegalese chef Pierre Thiam, buy fonio from smallholder farming communities, with a mission to create economic opportunity for them3. Yolélé de-hulls its fonio using traditional methods in West Africa, so the odd bit of grit or husk is normal1.

Handling

Fonio cooks in about five minutes, and one cup of dry grain makes about four cups cooked1. People say fonio never embarrasses the cook1. Unlike rice, it forgives: if it comes out soggy, cook off the extra liquid; if it is dry, add a spoonful of water, cover, and give it a minute more1.

  1. One cup of dry fonio makes about four cups cooked.
  2. Coat the grains with oil before adding water.
  3. Fluff with a fork and serve.

Uses, catalogued

Sauté diced onion and ginger in olive oil for three to five minutes, then fold in cooked fonio and turn off the heat1. The full method is its own piece: Curried Fonio Pilaf →

One part fonio to four parts water or milk, with a pinch of salt1. It cooks into a soft, warm cereal in minutes.

Fonio also works in veggie burgers, in tabbouleh, as bread crumbs, and in gluten-free baking1.

What it holds

Fonio asks very little of the cook and gives back a lot. A grain kept and passed on for thousands of years is worth keeping well: described honestly, credited to the people who grow it, and cooked often.

For more, read my piece for the Institute of Culinary Education: Fonio Grain: A Legacy of Sustainability and Flavor↗.

Sweet and baking

On the counter and in the fridge

Storage and cleanup

  • Glass jars, for buying in bulk
  • Beeswax wraps

  • Cotton or linen towels in place of paper
  • White vinegar and baking soda, for cleaning
  • A compost bin

Ground spices fade within a year or so. Buy small amounts, and buy whole when you can.

A few favorites

Kewpie

Japanese mayonnaise made with egg yolks and rice vinegar. Richer and tangier than American mayo.

Use it for dressings, sandwiches, roasted vegetables, and quick dips.

Black garlic

Whole garlic aged at low heat for weeks until the cloves turn black, soft, and sweet, with notes of balsamic and molasses.

Use it for mashing into butter, stirring into dressings and sauces, or spreading on toast.

Saffron honey

Honey infused with saffron threads. Floral, a little earthy, and golden.

Use it for yogurt, toast, roasted carrots, tea, or a honey vinaigrette.

Knives

KnifeWhat it’s for
Chef’s knife, 8 inchMost of your cutting: chopping, slicing, and dicing. The one worth spending on.
Paring knifeSmall work in your hand: peeling, trimming, and coring.
Serrated bread knifeAnything with a crust or a skin: bread, tomatoes, and cakes.
Santoku (optional)A Japanese all-purpose knife with a flatter edge, good for thin, even slices.
Boning knife (optional)Breaking down poultry and trimming meat.

Hone the edge often, sharpen it a few times a year, and wash knives by hand.

Pots and pans

PieceMaterialBest forCare
Skillet, 10 to 12 inchCast ironSearing, cornbread, and moving from stove to oven. Holds heat well.Dry it right away and wipe on a thin coat of oil. The seasoning builds as you cook.
Skillet, 10 to 12 inchStainless steelBrowning, pan sauces, and acidic foods like tomatoes.Heat the pan before adding oil to cut down on sticking. Safe to scrub.
SkilletCeramic nonstickEggs, pancakes, and delicate foods.Low to medium heat, and no metal utensils.
Dutch oven, 5 to 7 quartEnameled cast ironBraises, stews, soups, beans, and bread.Avoid heating it empty on high, and skip metal scrubbers on the enamel.
Saucepan, 2 to 3 quartStainless steelGrains, sauces, and reheating.Safe to scrub.
Stockpot, 8 quart or largerStainless steelStock, pasta, and big batches.Safe to scrub.
Sheet pansAluminumRoasting vegetables, sheet-pan dinners, and baking.Line with parchment for easy cleanup.

Other tools

Cutting boardsWood or bamboo, one kept for raw meat
Instant-read thermometerTakes the guessing out of doneness
Kitchen scaleMore accurate than cups, especially for baking
TongsTurning, tossing, and serving
Fish spatulaThin and flexible, useful for far more than fish
Wooden spoonsStirring without scratching
MicroplaneZest, garlic, ginger, and hard cheese
Bench scraperMoving chopped food from board to pan
Mixing bowlsA nesting set of three
Colander and fine-mesh strainerDraining pasta, rinsing grains
Measuring cups and spoonsFor recipes that need them
PeelerVegetables and quick ribbons

Where to start

If you’re buying today: a chef’s knife, a cutting board, a 12 inch skillet, a Dutch oven, a sheet pan, sea salt, a good oil, white vinegar, onions, garlic, and one grain. Everything else can come as you cook.

dek: A tiny West African grain that cooks in five minutes, forgives your mistakes, and carries thousands of years of farming with it.
html:
The relic

Fonio is easy to overlook. Each grain is tiny, and a bag of it looks more like sand than supper. But it has been prized across West Africa for more than 5,000 years1, and in Mali it is known as the seed of the universe, the grain at the root of all existence1.

This piece keeps it the way a reliquary keeps a relic: described, traced to where it comes from, and handled with care.

Catalog entry
ObjectFonio, a small grain
Also known asThe seed of the universe, in Mali
RegionWest Africa
Kept forMore than 5,000 years
Cooks inAbout five minutes
Yield1 cup dry makes about 4 cups cooked

Description

Fonio is an ancient grain1. Cooked, it turns light and fluffy, with a gentle nuttiness1. It is also gluten free2.

Provenance

Brands like Yolélé, co-founded by Senegalese chef Pierre Thiam, buy fonio from smallholder farming communities, with a mission to create economic opportunity for them3. Yolélé de-hulls its fonio using traditional methods in West Africa, so the odd bit of grit or husk is normal1.

Handling

Fonio cooks in about five minutes, and one cup of dry grain makes about four cups cooked1. People say fonio never embarrasses the cook1. Unlike rice, it forgives: if it comes out soggy, cook off the extra liquid; if it is dry, add a spoonful of water, cover, and give it a minute more1.

  1. One cup of dry fonio makes about four cups cooked.
  2. Coat the grains with oil before adding water.
  3. Fluff with a fork and serve.

Uses, catalogued

Sauté diced onion and ginger in olive oil for three to five minutes, then fold in cooked fonio and turn off the heat1. The full method is its own piece: Curried Fonio Pilaf →

One part fonio to four parts water or milk, with a pinch of salt1. It cooks into a soft, warm cereal in minutes.

Fonio also works in veggie burgers, in tabbouleh, as bread crumbs, and in gluten-free baking1.

What it holds

Fonio asks very little of the cook and gives back a lot. A grain kept and passed on for thousands of years is worth keeping well: described honestly, credited to the people who grow it, and cooked often.

For more, read my piece for the Institute of Culinary Education: Fonio Grain: A Legacy of Sustainability and Flavor↗.

title: The Systems Beneath: Understanding Foodshed Mapping
dek: A foodshed is the land and the routes that feed a place. Mapping it shows what holds, what breaks, and who ends up at the end of the line.
html:
1929. Walter Hedden borrows an idea from water and calls the area that feeds a city its foodshed.

1991. After decades of quiet, Arthur Getz revives the term in Permaculture Activist.

1996. Kloppenburg, Hendrickson, and Stevenson argue the foodshed can be a real unit for thought and action.

2009. Peters and colleagues define it as the area a population draws its food from.

2015. UC Merced researchers find existing cropland could feed up to 90 percent of Americans from within 100 miles.

2019. The USDA access atlas update adds measures based on whether households have a vehicle.

1929: The word

In 1929, Walter Hedden was trying to explain how a big city eats. He borrowed an idea from water and called it a foodshed1. A watershed is shaped by ridges and hills. Hedden pointed out that a foodshed is shaped mostly by money. Prices, freight, and markets decide where food flows, more than the land does1.

The word went quiet for decades. Arthur Getz brought it back in 19912, and in 1996 three researchers argued it could be more than a metaphor. It could be a real unit you study and act on3.

What it is
the area a population draws its food from4.
What a map can show
where food grows, how it moves, and where it never arrives.
What a map can't show yet
the relationships that keep it all running.

2015: What could stay local

In 2015, researchers at UC Merced↗ asked a blunt question. If existing cropland fed the people nearby, how far would it go5? Their answer was up to 90 percent of Americans, from food grown within 100 miles. Most areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of their people from within 50 miles5.

RadiusFindingWhat it means
50 milesMost areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of residentsLocal supply is possible for most places
100 milesUp to 90 percent of AmericansThe potential is high; today's routes rarely use it
Dense metrosGreater Los Angeles, up to about half within 100 milesBig cities still lean on long supply chains

Potential is not practice. Many farms serve markets far beyond the cities closest to them6. The land is there. The routes point somewhere else.

2019: Where food doesn't arrive

The other half of the map is access. USDA's Food Access Research Atlas↗ flags census tracts that are both low income and far from a supermarket7. The standard line is 1 mile in cities and 10 miles in rural areas, with versions at half a mile and 20 miles7.

Distance alone misses something. The 2019 update added measures based on vehicle access8, which changes the math for anyone who walks or takes the bus.

The numbers
Term coined1929, in How Great Cities Are Fed1
Local potential, 100 milesUp to 90 percent of Americans5
Local potential, 50 miles80 to 100 percent of residents in most areas5
Greater Los AngelesUp to about half within 100 miles5
Low access, urbanMore than 1 mile from a supermarket, with a stricter half-mile version7
Low access, ruralMore than 10 miles, with a looser 20-mile version7
Tract thresholdAt least 500 people or 33 percent of residents past the line7

The record, in order

Who's on it
USDA ERS, Food Access Atlas↗Maps census tracts that are both low income and far from a supermarket, at several distances7.
UC Merced, Campbell lab↗Modeled how much of the country could eat from cropland within 50 and 100 miles5.
Cornell, Peters et al.↗Traced the history of the term and laid out what foodshed analysis means4.
Kloppenburg, Hendrickson & Stevenson↗Argued the foodshed is a unit for both thought and action3.
A live, shared regional mapThe gap this project is working on. The pieces sit in separate studies and public datasets.

The idea has a long paper trail. A few places to start, plus one to watch:

1929 · Book
How Great Cities Are Fed ↗
Hedden traces the routes that fed a major city and gives the foodshed its name.
1996 · Agriculture and Human Values
Coming in to the Foodshed ↗
The paper that turned a metaphor into a way of studying food systems.
2015 · UC Merced
Local croplands could feed up to 90 percent ↗
Mapping how much of the country could eat from within 100 miles.
2021 · USDA ERS
Food Access Research Atlas, 2019 update ↗
Where supermarket access changed, tract by tract.
Video · YouTube
Video bookmark example ↗
Tap the image to play it here. Tap the title to open it on YouTube.

Mapping by season

My mapping work starts with three layers. Each one builds on the last.

Read across a year, the map keeps changing. What grows in July is gone by January, and the routes that carry it shift with the season. So each layer is drawn more than once, season by season.

1

Map where food grows. Farms, gardens, and growers come first: who grows what, how much, and in which season.

2

Trace how it moves. Aggregators, distributors, trucks, and markets. This is the hardest layer to see, so it comes from conversations with growers and distributors.

3

Find where access breaks. Public data does the heavy lifting here. The access atlas↗ shows where supermarkets are far away7, and vehicle access shows who can actually get there8.

The questionWhere does a region's food come from, and where does it fail to arrive?
What we knowMost areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of residents from within 50 miles5. Access gaps are mapped tract by tract7.
What's missingThe routes in between: who moves food, how far, and how often.

A foodshed map isn't the answer. It's a better question.

  2. 2

1929. Walter Hedden borrows an idea from water and calls the area that feeds a city its foodshed.

1991. After decades of quiet, Arthur Getz revives the term in Permaculture Activist.

1996. Kloppenburg, Hendrickson, and Stevenson argue the foodshed can be a real unit for thought and action.

2009. Peters and colleagues define it as the area a population draws its food from.

2015. UC Merced researchers find existing cropland could feed up to 90 percent of Americans from within 100 miles.

2019. The USDA access atlas update adds measures based on whether households have a vehicle.

1929: The word

In 1929, Walter Hedden was trying to explain how a big city eats. He borrowed an idea from water and called it a foodshed1. A watershed is shaped by ridges and hills. Hedden pointed out that a foodshed is shaped mostly by money. Prices, freight, and markets decide where food flows, more than the land does1.

The word went quiet for decades. Arthur Getz brought it back in 19912, and in 1996 three researchers argued it could be more than a metaphor. It could be a real unit you study and act on3.

What it is
the area a population draws its food from4.
What a map can show
where food grows, how it moves, and where it never arrives.
What a map can't show yet
the relationships that keep it all running.

2015: What could stay local

In 2015, researchers at UC Merced↗ asked a blunt question. If existing cropland fed the people nearby, how far would it go5? Their answer was up to 90 percent of Americans, from food grown within 100 miles. Most areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of their people from within 50 miles5.

RadiusFindingWhat it means
50 milesMost areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of residentsLocal supply is possible for most places
100 milesUp to 90 percent of AmericansThe potential is high; today's routes rarely use it
Dense metrosGreater Los Angeles, up to about half within 100 milesBig cities still lean on long supply chains

Potential is not practice. Many farms serve markets far beyond the cities closest to them6. The land is there. The routes point somewhere else.

2019: Where food doesn't arrive

The other half of the map is access. USDA's Food Access Research Atlas↗ flags census tracts that are both low income and far from a supermarket7. The standard line is 1 mile in cities and 10 miles in rural areas, with versions at half a mile and 20 miles7.

Distance alone misses something. The 2019 update added measures based on vehicle access8, which changes the math for anyone who walks or takes the bus.

The numbers
Term coined1929, in How Great Cities Are Fed1
Local potential, 100 milesUp to 90 percent of Americans5
Local potential, 50 miles80 to 100 percent of residents in most areas5
Greater Los AngelesUp to about half within 100 miles5
Low access, urbanMore than 1 mile from a supermarket, with a stricter half-mile version7
Low access, ruralMore than 10 miles, with a looser 20-mile version7
Tract thresholdAt least 500 people or 33 percent of residents past the line7

The record, in order

Who's on it

UC Merced, Campbell lab↗Modeled how much of the country could eat from cropland within 50 and 100 miles5.

A live, shared regional mapThe gap this project is working on. The pieces sit in separate studies and public datasets.

The idea has a long paper trail. A few places to start, plus one to watch:

Mapping by season

My mapping work starts with three layers. Each one builds on the last.

Read across a year, the map keeps changing. What grows in July is gone by January, and the routes that carry it shift with the season. So each layer is drawn more than once, season by season.

1

Map where food grows. Farms, gardens, and growers come first: who grows what, how much, and in which season.

2

Trace how it moves. Aggregators, distributors, trucks, and markets. This is the hardest layer to see, so it comes from conversations with growers and distributors.

3

Find where access breaks. Public data does the heavy lifting here. The access atlas↗ shows where supermarkets are far away7, and vehicle access shows who can actually get there8.

The questionWhere does a region's food come from, and where does it fail to arrive?
What we knowMost areas could feed 80 to 100 percent of residents from within 50 miles5. Access gaps are mapped tract by tract7.
What's missingThe routes in between: who moves food, how far, and how often.

A foodshed map isn't the answer. It's a better question.

Visual Research: The brief

Collecting materials for a client branding project focused on regenerative agriculture. The goal was a visual system combining earthy tones with living greens.

The clientA regenerative agriculture brand
The askLook like soil and growth, not like a wellness label
The guardrailVisuals can't promise more than the farming does. The Regenerative Organic Certified standard, set up in 2017, rests on soil health, animal welfare, and social fairness11.

Mood board & color study

Moodboards feel like instinct. I wanted to know what they actually said, so I measured them.

4

Collect. Two boards: one for color, one for texture and objects. Paper, seed packets, linen, soil, dried leaves, old maps, hand-drawn type. Anything that felt like it came out of the ground or out of someone's hands.

5

Measure. Every pixel on both boards got sorted by hue, in narrow bands around the color wheel9. The result looks like this:

What the boards said

Mostly neutral
about 48 percent of every pixel was paper, linen, bone, or shadow9.
Warm and narrow
92 percent of the remaining color sat between red-orange and olive, 10 to 70 degrees9.
One loud band
40 to 50 degrees, ochre and mustard, held 19 percent of all pixels on its own9.
No blue
the whole blue range came in under 1 percent9.
6

Extract. Next, the boards got reduced to their most common colors9. The bright white board background is left out.

Extracted palette
Paper#ece7da · 14.9% of pixels9
Wheat#c2b89b · 13.6% of pixels9
Soil#6f5e49 · 13.1% of pixels9
Loam#392315 · 12.3% of pixels9
Linen#d7d5c7 · 10.9% of pixels9
Dry sage#9b967b · 10.4% of pixels9
7

Correct. The measurement showed a gap. The boards had soil and paper, but no living green. So the working palette adds it on purpose, and every swatch gets tested next to the others, never alone. The same color reads differently depending on what surrounds it10.

The Planting Year: Seasonal Timeline

Mapping the invisible calendar that governs food systems, not just climate seasons, but the deeper rhythms of soil, water, labor, and harvest cycles.

Spring (March–May)
Soil prep, seed germination, water management, labor surge in transplant season. Corresponds to numerological cycles of new growth.
Summer (June–August)
Peak production, daily harvests, heat stress management, irrigation intensity. Full system activation.
Fall (Sept–Nov)
Transition crops, season extension, soil amendment, preparation for dormancy. Harvest celebration cycles.
Winter (Dec–Feb)
Rest, planning, system assessment, infrastructure work. Internal cycles and preparation.
